strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear legal context (EU AI Act, litigation); addresses real need for data provenance auditing
Sound theoretical foundation: cue-reply split design is clever, watermark generation constraints are rigorous, FPR-bounded ranking test provides formal guarantees (FPR ≤ k/K)
Text-preservation via invisible Unicode is minimal invasiveness improvement over prior work requiring visible modifications
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: systematic variation of collection size, dataset size, and concurrent watermarks with honest error reporting
Strong empirical results: <0.1% failure rate with 50 documents; >45% detection with 0.33% marked data; 100% TPR@0% FPR in ranking test
Scalability via large watermark space (|W| ≈ 1.86M) supporting many users without collisions, addressing limitation of homoglyph-based approaches
Black-box operability requires only text I/O; works with proprietary APIs unlike grey-box methods requiring probability access
Honest and comprehensive limitations discussion acknowledging scope constraints and robustness gaps
Reproducibility supported by promised code release, detailed hyperparameters, and evaluation scripts
weaknesses: Limited scope to fine-tuning only—does not apply to pretraining or RLHF which account for most LLM capability development; significantly reduces real-world applicability

Brittleness to adversarial transformations is unaddressed—vulnerable to aggressive normalization, sanitization, zero-width filtering, and paraphrasing, yet systematic robustness evaluation is deferred to future work; critical gap for copyright protection use cases
No empirical comparison with prior work (Wei et al. [36], Meeus et al. [10])—unclear how detection rates, invasiveness, and scalability compare; difficult to assess relative merit
Reliance on trusted third party creates operational burden and governance challenges for adoption; solutions (append-only logs, blockchains) are mentioned but deferred

Limited evaluation scope: only 2 open-source models (no proprietary APIs like GPT-4/Claude), 2 text domains (blogs/poetry; missing news, academic papers, code), only LoRA fine-tuning (not full FT, QLoRA); generalization claims somewhat overstated
Completeness guarantee is purely empirical with no theoretical bound on false-negative rate; dependence on model memorization and fine-tuning dynamics is not characterized
Post-hoc watermarking only—requires watermarking before training, cannot retroactively detect unmarked documents; limits applicability to new workflows
Practical adoption path unclear—requires coordination between authors, TTP, and providers; incentive alignment and governance mechanisms entirely left to future work
Detection performance varies significantly across models/domains (Mistral/Poetry requires 40-50 documents vs LLaMA/Blog requiring 20+); scalability to single-document scenarios unclear
Multi-watermark interference shows concerning degradation in worst case (95%→72% on LLaMA-Poems with 12 watermarks), limiting practical scalability despite overall positive results

strengths: Well-motivated and timely problem addressing data provenance and copyright issues for LLMs with clear legal context
Truly text-preserving approach using invisible Unicode—genuine advantage over prior methods requiring visible text modifications
Formal false-positive rate guarantees via ranking test against counterfactual watermarks, important for legal/forensic applications
Comprehensive empirical study examining sensitivity to collection size, dataset size, concurrent watermarks, and detection reliability
Black-box operability requiring only text I/O makes method applicable to real-world deployment scenarios
Exponential watermark space supports scalable multi-user scenarios with uniqueness constraints
Promises reproducibility through code release and detailed experimental setup in appendices
weaknesses: Critical robustness failure: method is brittle to standard text transformations (PDF-to-text, OCR, normalization, sanitization) that are ubiquitous in ML pipelines; authors acknowledge but defer to future work despite this being disqualifying for legal evidence application
Severely restricted scope—only works for fine-tuning via LoRA, explicitly not applicable to pretraining or RLHF; most deployed LLMs use these paradigms
Weak detection rates in realistic scenarios: 0-1.3% for Mistral-Poems with 30-40 documents; degradation to 72% with multiple concurrent watermarks; claimed 45% rates only under favorable conditions

Artificial evaluation of false-positive bound: 100% TPR@0% FPR is artifact of 200-token output limit and ~10^-5 theoretical collision probability; no validation under longer outputs or adversarial watermark selection
Single trusted third party (TTP) dependency creates operational burden and trust vulnerability; concrete deployment model and governance never addressed
No evaluation against adaptive adversaries despite trivial defenses (zero-width filtering, paraphrasing, normalization); threat model incomplete
Incomplete problem formulation: doesn't handle partial document inclusion, data augmentation, deduplication, or semantic equivalents from training pipeline
Moderate novelty: invisible Unicode watermarking, ranking tests, and cue-reply splits individually known; contribution is primarily engineering these for LLM fine-tuning
Experimental limitations: small scale (50-60 marked docs vs. thousands in real copyright cases), limited diversity (2 datasets, 2 models), missing ablations, no baseline comparisons
Verification budget not characterized: no clear guidance on query cost for practical audits; completeness depends on poorly-specified λ and X parameters
Legal and ethical concerns minimized: imperceptible modification without informed consent is ethically questionable; liability and court admissibility unaddressed
Misleading presentation: '100% TPR@0% FPR' stated without adequate caveats; limitations scattered across Section V and footnotes rather than prominently discussed

strengths: Addresses timely and critical problem in data governance and copyright protection for LLMs with strong legal/societal motivation
Text-preserving invisible Unicode watermarking is elegant and practical—preserves visible text byte-for-byte while maximizing watermark capacity
Provides provable false-positive rate bounds (FPR ≤ k/K) via ranking test against counterfactual watermarks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two models and datasets with systematic ablations of collection size, dataset size, and unique watermarks
Exceptional empirical results: 100% TPR @ 0% FPR across 18,810 challenges; detection remains >45% even with <0.33% watermarked data
Black-box operability with text I/O only makes it practical for proprietary and closed-weight models
Scalable watermark space (~1.86M unique watermarks) enables multi-user attribution without collisions
Multi-watermark experiments demonstrate modest interference across most settings (only one significant drop to 72%)
Honest and detailed discussion of limitations in Section V with proposed mitigations
Promises code and utilities release for reproducibility
weaknesses: Robustness is a critical vulnerability: brittle to common transformations (zero-width filtering, aggressive normalization, OCR, paraphrasing); undermines claim of providing 'credible proof' for copyright litigation
Completeness guarantees are only empirical—no theoretical proof provided; detection rates vary significantly (0% Mistral/Poems @ 30 docs to >90% LLaMA/Blog1k)
Deliberately scoped to LoRA-based fine-tuning; completeness not claimed for pretraining, RLHF, or full fine-tuning with different recipes
Evaluated on only two open-source 7B models; no assessment on closed-weight APIs (GPT-4, Claude) or instruction-tuned/RLHF variants
Trusted Third Party requirement creates operational burden and centralization risk; practical deployment model remains unclear
Multi-watermark validation limited to 12 concurrent watermarks; scalability claims to 'millions of users' rest on theoretical space size rather than empirical evidence
Document chunking simplified to δ = ⌈Δ/2⌉ for convenience without principled justification; unclear if realistic
Sparse detection signal: reply is only 12 invisible characters in 200-token output; sensitivity to output length limitations unclear
Legal evidentiary thresholds for 'credible proof' remain undefined; informed consent mechanisms proposed but not specified
Limited comparative evaluation: only one text-preserving baseline cited; no direct empirical comparison with other DPA/watermarking methods
